entries.test: Public AI investment, valuation and financing data would show whether the boom suffered a sharp, broad collapse soon after September 2025.
entries.note: “Near future” supplies no definite deadline.

entries.test: Repeated controlled model runs and decoding experiments would show whether probabilistic generation prevents consistent results.

entries.note: “Broken digital product” functions here as a dismissive characterization.

entries.test: Documented workplace deployments and independent evaluations would show whether contemporary LLMs could perform coders’ jobs without a human replacement doing the substantive work.
entries.note: He answers his own question explicitly.

entries.test: Public production records and capability demonstrations would show whether Sora could substitute for actors or animators in actual production work at publication.
Public employment studies and documented displacement cases available at publication would show whether there was evidence of AI replacing workers at scale.
entries.note: The surrounding paragraph supplies “at scale,” but “nobody appears to be able to prove it” is weaker than an unqualified absence of proof.

entries.test: Documented AI-related job losses classified by occupation would show whether white collar workers or software engineers were among those displaced.
entries.note: His subsequent examples create tension with the broad white collar exclusion.
“Authentic” could mean genuine felt emotion or convincing prose; these require different tests.
The claim attributes private purposes to dealmakers rather than establishing the deals’ effects.

entries.test: OpenAI’s available funding, financial statements and contractual payment requirements at publication would show whether it could finance the Oracle commitment and required construction.

entries.note: The source says existing demand “doesn’t necessarily translate” into large business spending; the proposition removes that qualification.

entries.test: Public investment totals and company financial results through publication would establish cumulative generative AI investment and whether any model or model-based product company was profitable.
Full-year 2025 generative AI company revenues and financial results would settle the revenue estimate and loss claim.
entries.note: The post later explicitly corrects the industry revenue estimate to approximately $55 billion, or $61 billion including neoclouds. The $44 billion figure does not represent his final position.

entries.test: OpenAI and Anthropic’s costs over the preceding two years and Uber’s cumulative cash burn would establish the amounts and comparison.
Microsoft’s paid Microsoft 365 Copilot license count at publication divided by 440 million would show whether penetration was below 3%.

entries.note: Data center size and what revenue would “justify” one are unspecified and vary substantially.

entries.test: Public contract terms, spending commitments and financing announcements at publication would establish OpenAI’s obligations and disclosed payment plan.
Industry financing, company failures and investment data would show whether generative AI underwent the predicted broad industry collapse.
entries.note: The metaphor reiterates the post’s explicit collapse forecast.

entries.test: Independent repeated-task evaluations would show whether contemporary LLMs reliably followed user instructions and completed requested work.
Controlled evaluations varying task complexity and step count would show whether error accumulation prevents agents from reliably completing autonomous work.
Repeated independent evaluations of reasoning-enhanced LLMs would establish whether they still produce incorrect or inconsistent results.
Public financial results at publication would show whether AI operations outside NVIDIA and GPU resellers generated profits.
entries.note: “Make money” means profit in this context.
“Most aggressive,” “destructive” and “more ridiculous” provide no concrete comparative commitment here.
“Set up to fail” and “all comes down to” do not define an agreed outcome or degree of dependence.

entries.test: CoreWeave, Nebius and Lambda’s 2025 revenues broken down by customer would establish revenue excluding the named companies.
entries.note: The surrounding calculation uses estimated full-year 2025 revenue.

entries.test: Public neocloud financial results, NVIDIA funding agreements, debt documents and GPU purchases would show profitability and whether NVIDIA support enabled borrowing for its GPUs.
entries.note: The proposition changes “will” into an assertion of present funding activity.

entries.test: Public neocloud customer contracts, customer finances and compute demand would show whether lack of affordable demand explains the absence of major independent customers.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion excludes hyperscalers as independent sources of demand.

entries.test: 2025 industry revenues and OpenAI’s revenue and compute spending would establish whether the combined OpenAI-linked amount represented about half of the stated industry total.
entries.note: The 50% calculation includes OpenAI’s spending as other companies’ revenue and refers to full-year 2025. “Bad company” is an accompanying value judgment.

entries.test: OpenAI’s Oracle payment schedule, other cash requirements, revenues and financing through September 2029 would establish the external capital required under that deal scenario.
entries.note: His estimate is based on incorporating the Oracle deal; it does not say all $290 billion is solely for Oracle payments.
No agreed threshold defines a “healthy, stable” industry.

entries.test: Public company accounts, model operating-cost trends and product revenues would show whether rising delivery costs and insufficient monetization explain generative AI losses.
Anthropic and OpenAI’s revenues and cash burn through publication would establish the stated year-to-date amounts.
entries.note: The quoted projections are full-year figures; “below projections” misleadingly implies a comparable year-to-date target.

entries.test: Public financial reports and funding disclosures for other AI startups would show their gross margins and financial distress at publication.
Published user-level revenue and serving-cost studies, together with cost-control demonstrations, would show whether every generative AI user is unprofitable because costs cannot be controlled.

entries.note: “Likely” qualifies the architectural explanation, not directly the inability to limit activity; the proposition moves that hedge.

entries.test: Anthropic’s reported 2025 financial results and cash burn would establish its losses and whether burn reached billions of dollars.

entries.note: “Disaster” is an evaluative verdict without a specified factual threshold.

entries.test: Independent software-building evaluations and production deployments would show whether coding LLMs reliably produce working software without substantive human correction.
Public AI business unit economics, cost trends and pricing changes would show whether high and rising model costs prevent conventional routes to profitability.
entries.note: The surrounding text defines the “profit lever” as converting a growing software business to profitability.

entries.test: Public router architecture, caching documentation and cost comparisons available at publication would show whether net savings had been established.
entries.note: He asserts uncertainty about savings, not that the router definitely loses money.

entries.test: Claude Code’s monthly revenue and attributable operating costs around the reported July 2025 run rate would establish the revenue and profitability claim.
entries.note: The amount comes from a July annualized revenue report, not a new September measurement.

entries.test: Public labor-market research and documented employer staffing decisions would show whether AI replacement contributed to software engineers’ difficulty finding work.
entries.note: The checkable core is the denial of displacement, without requiring proof of journalists’ intentions.

entries.test: A documented deployment in which coding LLMs reliably replace software engineers’ substantive jobs would falsify the never-replacement prediction.
entries.note: This is Zitron’s own summary heading, not one of the preceding engineers’ quotations.

entries.test: Independent software engineering evaluations varying codebase context and adaptation requirements would test the asserted capability limits and their explanation.
entries.note: He adopts the explanation in his own voice while crediting Brown for part of it.

entries.test: Publicly documented AI replacements of software engineers and independent capability evaluations available at publication would test both the absence of proof and claimed inability.
Public evaluations across increasing coding-task complexity would show whether hallucinations and failures increase.
Independent end-to-end software engineering trials with reported costs would establish whether generative AI could perform the job and at what expense.
Controlled studies comparing engineers’ completion times with and without coding LLMs would establish their effect on speed.
Public evidence of established, useful non-coding LLM applications would test whether coding was effectively the only clear use case at publication.
Microsoft’s August 2025 Copilot active licensed-user figures and Microsoft 365 subscriber totals would establish the count and percentage.
entries.note: Reporting a source’s factual finding in his own prose is not quoting that source’s words.

entries.test: Public customer contracts or documented paid purchases below $30 per month would establish that some Microsoft 365 Copilot users received discounts.
Microsoft’s product announcements and published accounts of the integration decision would show whether Copilot performance problems led to adoption of Anthropic models.
entries.note: “Disaster” is evaluative, but the asserted product decision and causal explanation have a factual core.

entries.test: Published Microsoft enterprise Copilot GPU utilization measurements for the relevant period would establish whether utilization was approximately 60%.
Public enterprise GPU workload and revenue data would establish the prevalence and commercial scale of non-AI uses compared with fiber’s applications.
Public AI customer spending, utilization and contracted demand at publication would show whether substantial demand existed relative to infrastructure investment.

entries.note: He explicitly presents the annual spending total as a guess.

entries.test: Public construction, equipment and commissioning budgets for comparable fully equipped 1GW AI data centers would establish whether $10 billion was sufficient.
Public NVIDIA deal terms and realized 10GW buildout costs would show whether a $50 billion per GW cost required $500 billion of spending to unlock the investment.
entries.note: The cost assumption is a stated antecedent, not probability language.
“Threatens the future” specifies neither a capital shortfall nor an outcome that would settle the claim.

entries.test: If OpenAI survives to 2029, its cumulative reported cash burn by then would establish whether it exceeded $290 billion.
OpenAI’s continued operation or cessation before 2029 would settle the survival prediction.
entries.note: “I do not believe it will” expresses his directional prediction, without an explicit chance or possibility hedge.

entries.test: OpenAI’s financing, contract payments, cumulative cash burn and profitability would establish whether it could fund its obligations and avoid the predicted financial outcome.
entries.note: The record combines present financial assertions with an undated burn and profitability prediction.
He endorses an unlikelihood assessment, not NVIDIA’s quoted deployment forecast.

entries.test: Public investment payments and completion or termination of the existing NVIDIA-OpenAI arrangement would show whether NVIDIA ultimately provided $100 billion.
OpenAI’s available cash and financing at publication compared with its Oracle payment obligations would establish whether it had the required money.
entries.note: The present tense retains the source’s current-relationship scope.
Ranking the boom among history’s most egregious wastes is a judgment of worth.

entries.test: Longitudinal GPU failure records, successor hardware performance and resale prices would test the predicted breakdown, obsolescence and car-like depreciation.
entries.note: “Rapidly” replaces the specific new-car comparison and omits the explicit “five years or later” qualification.

entries.test: Public customer revenues and utilization demonstrating sustained commercial demand sufficient to support the generative AI buildout would falsify the never-demand prediction.
entries.note: Context concerns economically sustaining demand, not whether anyone uses AI.
The promised “revolution” has no agreed operational meaning or threshold.

entries.test: OpenAI’s reported 2025 cash burn and cumulative burn through 2030 would establish whether they reached at least $8 billion and nearly $1 trillion respectively.
entries.note: The proposition weakens the explicit qualification “if my estimates are right” to an attribution. The 2025 component is already due.
The central claim attributes a private purpose and awareness to NVIDIA; “farce” adds an evaluative label.

entries.test: Historical reliability evaluations and financial results would show whether generative AI had demonstrated dependable operation and sustained profitability before publication.
entries.note: “Sustainable” refers to the business economics in this context.
OpenAI’s eventual failure is independently testable, but the comparative damage from earlier versus later failure requires a counterfactual.

entries.test: OpenAI’s subsequent fundraising and disclosed private-credit borrowing would show whether it continued absorbing capital and entered private credit.
entries.note: “I expect” is a firm expectation under the specified rules.

entries.test: Public global private-capital dry-powder estimates at publication would establish whether available private capital was below $325 billion.
entries.note: “I believe” presents a factual conclusion here, rather than a stated probability.

entries.test: Following an OpenAI collapse, public output, employment and financial-stability data would show whether its systemic economic damage was less severe than the pandemic or global financial crisis.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion supplies the antecedent of OpenAI failing.

entries.test: If the described coverage continues, public retail-investor and retirement-fund losses linked to the promoted AI investments would test the predicted financial harm.
entries.note: The forecast is explicitly tied to continued media promotion.

entries.test: A broad collapse in AI valuations, financing and investment would establish the predicted bursting of the AI bubble.
Public evidence tracing AI-promotional coverage to ordinary investors’ exposure and resulting losses during a bubble collapse would test the claimed causal harm.
entries.note: The proposition drops the source’s universal “every single” and exclusive “only” wording.
